questions.question: How do you read a Java stack trace to find the source of an error?
questions.title: How to Read a Java Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Read the first line for the exception type and message, then scan the 'at' lines top-to-bottom to find the first line pointing to your own code — that is usually where the bug is.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can independently diagnose errors without hand-holding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading stack traces top-down through all framework lines instead of jumping to your own code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the structure: exception → caused-by chain → identifying user code vs framework code

sections.title: Anatomy of a Stack Trace
sections.content: A **stack trace** is Java's crime scene report — it tells you exactly what went wrong and where. When an exception occurs, the JVM freezes the current state and prints a reverse chronological list of method calls that led to the failure. Think of it like a breadcrumb trail: the top shows where the exception was thrown, and each subsequent line shows the caller that invoked it. The key skill is **filtering signal from noise** — in a Spring Boot app, you'll see 40+ lines of framework internals, but your bug is in one of the 3-5 lines from your own package. Reading a stack trace efficiently means understanding this structure: **exception declaration** (type and message), **your application frames** (the 'at' lines with your package name), and **framework frames** (Spring, Hibernate, Tomcat). Freshers often get overwhelmed and try to understand every line. Instead, you scan for your package name, jump to that line number in your IDE, and inspect the state at that point. The rest is just context showing how execution reached your code.

sections.title: Reading a Real Stack Trace
Key Points
content: **Exception header**: First line shows exception type (e.g. NullPointerException) and descriptive message
**'at' frames**: Each line starting with 'at' represents one method call in the execution chain
**Line numbers**: The number after the colon (e.g. OrderService.java:45) tells you exactly where to look
**Package filtering**: Your application code appears under your package (com.example); framework code is everything else
**Top-down order**: Read from top (where exception was thrown) down to bottom (main or framework entry point)
**IDE integration**: Most IDEs let you click stack trace lines to jump directly to that code location
**Framework noise**: Lines from java.base, org.springframework, org.hibernate are usually not your bug — skip them

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I see a stack trace, I start with the first line to understand what went wrong — it tells me the exception type like NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException and often includes a helpful message. Then I scan down the at lines looking for my own package name. In a Spring Boot app, you'll see tons of framework lines from Spring and Tomcat, but I skip those because my bug is almost never in the framework. Once I find my package, say com.example.order.OrderService, I note the line number — that's where the exception originated in my code. I go to that exact line in my IDE and check the state: which variable could be null, which method might throw that exception, what input could cause this. If it's a NullPointerException, I look at every object reference on that line to see which one is null. One mistake freshers make is trying to read every single framework line, but that's a waste of time. The bug is in your code ninety-nine percent of the time. Focus on your package lines, understand what your code was trying to do at that moment, and you'll find the issue fast. Modern IDEs even let you click the stack trace to jump right to the problematic line, which saves a ton of time.

questions.question: What does 'Caused by' in a Java stack trace mean and how do you use it?
questions.title: Caused By — Nested Exceptions in Java Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: 'Caused by' shows the original exception that triggered a wrapper exception — you should always read the innermost 'Caused by' first because it contains the true root cause.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to navigate real-world stack traces which almost always have nested exceptions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only reading the top-level exception and missing the real cause buried in a Caused-by
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain exception chaining with initCause() — shows deeper understanding

sections.title: Exception Chaining and Root Causes
sections.content: **Exception chaining** is Java's way of preserving context when you wrap one exception inside another. Imagine an onion: the outer layer is a high-level business exception like OrderProcessingException, but peel it back and you find the real problem — a ConstraintViolationException from the database layer. The **Caused by** section in a stack trace shows this nested structure. Why does this matter? Because the top-level exception often just says "something went wrong," while the innermost exception tells you exactly what: database connection timeout, file not found, unique constraint violation. Freshers often stop reading after the first exception, but that's like diagnosing a patient by only checking their temperature and ignoring the blood test. In production Spring Boot apps, you'll see chains three or four levels deep: a controller catches a service exception, which wraps a repository exception, which wraps a JDBC exception. The **root cause** is always at the bottom of the chain. Java provides this through Throwable's initCause() method and constructors that accept a cause parameter, creating a linked list of exceptions.

sections.title: Exception Chain in Action
Key Points
content: **Caused by**: Keyword introducing the wrapped exception that triggered the current exception
**Root cause**: The innermost Caused by entry — this is the original problem that started everything
**Exception wrapping**: Common pattern where service/controller layers catch low-level exceptions and rethrow with business context
**Reading order**: Start at the top to understand business context, then jump to the bottom for technical root cause
**initCause()**: Java method that chains exceptions together, linking cause to wrapper
**Throwable chain**: Each exception can have exactly one cause, forming a singly-linked list
**Framework wrapping**: Spring and Hibernate often wrap JDBC exceptions, adding three or four layers to the chain

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I see Caused by in a stack trace, I know there's an exception chain — meaning one exception wrapped another. The top-level exception usually gives business context, like OrderException saying an order failed to process. But the real technical reason is buried deeper. I always scroll down to find the innermost Caused by because that's the root cause. For example, the top might say DataAccessException, which is generic, but if I scroll down I might find SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException with a message about duplicate keys. That tells me exactly what went wrong: I tried to insert a duplicate record. This happens a lot in Spring Boot because the framework wraps low-level exceptions. A database error gets wrapped by Hibernate, then wrapped again by Spring's data layer, and finally wrapped by my service class. Each layer adds context, but the original error is at the bottom. One mistake freshers make is reading only the first exception and missing the actual cause. It's like asking someone why they're late and they say car trouble, but you need to ask again to learn the tire was flat. Always read the full chain, especially the last Caused by. That's where the actionable information lives.

questions.question: How do you read a NullPointerException stack trace in Java?
questions.title: Reading a NullPointerException Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Find the 'at' line pointing to your code, note the line number, go to that line, and identify which object on that line could be null — Java 14+ even tells you the exact variable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical debugging ability — NullPointerException is the most common Java exception
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Randomly adding null checks everywhere instead of pinpointing which reference is null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java 14 Helpful NullPointerExceptions that name the exact null variable

sections.title: Diagnosing NullPointerException from Stack Traces
sections.content: **NullPointerException** (NPE) is the most common exception freshers encounter, and reading its stack trace is a fundamental debugging skill. An NPE means you tried to use an object reference that points to nothing — like trying to open a door when there's no door. The stack trace tells you exactly where this happened: which class, which method, which line. Before Java 14, the message was generic (just "NullPointerException"), forcing you to inspect every variable on that line. But **Java 14 introduced Helpful NullPointerExceptions**, which pinpoint the exact expression that was null, like "Cannot invoke Customer.getName() because customer is null." This is a game-changer for debugging. The process is straightforward: scan the stack trace for your package name, note the line number, open that file, and examine every object dereference (dot operator) on that line. The null reference is one of them. Think of it like finding a broken link in a chain — the stack trace tells you which link broke, and you inspect that link to see why it's null (uninitialized field, empty Optional, failed database lookup).

sections.title: Java 14 Helpful NPE Messages
Key Points
content: **NPE location**: Stack trace shows the exact line where you dereferenced a null pointer
**Java 14 improvement**: Helpful NullPointerExceptions name the exact null variable or method call
**Dot operator**: Every dot in a chain (customer.getAddress().getCity()) is a potential NPE point
**Common causes**: Uninitialized fields, failed Optional.orElse(null), database returning no result
**Fixing strategy**: Don't just add null checks everywhere — understand why the value is null in the first place
**Optional pattern**: Use Optional.ofNullable() and orElseThrow() to make null handling explicit
**Debugging tip**: In IDE debugger, hover over each subexpression on the NPE line to see which is null

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I see a NullPointerException stack trace, I first look for the at line with my package name and note the line number. That tells me exactly where the null dereference happened. I go to that line and check every object reference — every variable, every method call that returns an object. One of those is null. If I'm running Java 14 or later, the error message actually tells me which one. It'll say something like Cannot invoke getName because customer is null, which is super helpful. Before Java 14, I'd have to check each reference manually, maybe by adding breakpoints or print statements. Once I know which reference is null, I trace backward to understand why. Did I forget to initialize a field? Did a database lookup return empty? Did I use Optional.orElse with null? The fix isn't just slapping an if-not-null check everywhere. I need to understand the root cause. If customer should never be null at that point, then I should fail earlier with a clear error message. Or if it can be null, I should use Optional or check it before dereferencing. The key is reading the stack trace to find the exact line, then reasoning about why that specific reference is null at that moment in execution.

questions.question: How do you identify your own code versus framework code in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Identifying Your Code vs Framework Code in a Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Your code appears under your package name in the 'at' lines; everything else is framework or library code — focus on your package lines first because that's where your bug lives.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical skill — candidates who can't filter framework noise waste time in wrong places
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to understand every Spring/Hibernate line in a stack trace instead of jumping to application code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention IntelliJ's 'Hide framework stacks' feature that collapses library frames

sections.title: Filtering Your Code from Framework Internals
sections.content: In a Spring Boot application, a single HTTP request can trigger a stack trace with 50+ frames: Tomcat servlet handling, Spring MVC dispatching, transaction management, Hibernate ORM, JDBC drivers. Ninety-five percent of this is **framework plumbing** — code you didn't write and generally don't need to debug. Your bug is almost always in **your application code**, identifiable by your package name (e.g., com.example, org.mycompany). The skill is **visual scanning**: your eyes should skip over org.springframework, org.hibernate, java.base, and lock onto your package. Think of it like reading a book with footnotes — the main story is your code, and the footnotes are framework details. Modern IDEs understand this: IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse can **collapse framework frames** into a single line saying "52 more," letting you focus on your code. This filtering skill is critical because freshers waste hours trying to understand why Spring called a particular reflection method, when the real issue is their controller passed a null parameter. Framework code is battle-tested and rarely the problem; your code is new and likely contains the bug.

sections.title: Identifying Application Code in Stack Trace
Key Points
content: **Package identification**: Your code lives under your organization's package (com.example, org.mycompany)
**Framework packages**: org.springframework, org.hibernate, javax.servlet are not your code
**JDK internals**: java.base, jdk.internal, sun.reflect are low-level Java runtime — skip these
**Bug probability**: Ninety-five percent of bugs are in your code, not in mature frameworks
**IDE filtering**: IntelliJ and Eclipse can hide framework frames automatically in stack traces
**... N more**: This notation means the IDE collapsed N additional framework frames
**Visual pattern**: Train your eyes to skip lines starting with org.springframework and lock onto your package

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I read a stack trace, I scan the at lines looking for my package name. In a Spring Boot project, that's usually something like com.example or org.mycompany. Everything else — lines starting with org.springframework, org.hibernate, java.base — is framework code. I skip those because my bug is almost certainly not in Spring's internals. The framework is well-tested and used by millions of developers. My code is brand new and way more likely to have issues. So I focus on the lines with my package. Typically there are two or three of those in a stack of fifty lines. Those are my entry points for debugging. Once I identify my code, I look at the line numbers and think about what those methods do. One practical tip: most IDEs let you configure stepping filters to automatically hide framework packages during debugging. In IntelliJ, you can set it to collapse Spring and Hibernate frames, so your stack view shows only your application code. This saves tons of time. Instead of scrolling through forty lines of Spring reflection code, you immediately see your controller called your service, your service called the repository, and boom — there's the bug. Learn your package name, train your eyes to find it fast, and ignore the rest.

questions.question: What does a StackOverflowError stack trace look like and what causes it?
questions.title: StackOverflowError — What It Looks Like and Why It Happens
questions.direct_answer: StackOverflowError occurs when infinite recursion fills the call stack; its trace shows the same method repeated hundreds of times, and the fix is to add a base case to the recursion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of call stack mechanics and recursion
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that it's an Error not an Exception, and generally should not be caught

sections.title: Understanding StackOverflowError
sections.content: **StackOverflowError** is a JVM Error indicating the **call stack** has exceeded its maximum depth. The call stack is a memory region storing method call frames — each time you call a method, Java pushes a new frame onto the stack with local variables and return address. When the method returns, Java pops that frame. The stack has a fixed size (default around 1 MB, configurable via -Xss flag). If you call methods recursively without ever returning, the stack keeps growing until it runs out of space, and the JVM throws StackOverflowError. The telltale sign in a stack trace is **repetition**: the same method appears hundreds or thousands of times. This almost always means **infinite recursion** — a method calling itself with no base case to stop. Think of it like mirrors facing each other, reflecting infinitely. It's not the same as OutOfMemoryError, which affects the heap where objects live. StackOverflowError is about the call stack where method invocations live. Importantly, it's an **Error**, not an Exception, meaning it represents an abnormal condition you generally shouldn't catch or recover from — you fix the code instead.

sections.title: StackOverflowError from Missing Base Case
Key Points
content: **Call stack**: Memory region storing method invocation frames; each call pushes a frame, each return pops one
**Stack size**: Default around 1 MB per thread, configurable with JVM flag -Xss (e.g., -Xss2m for 2 MB)
**Error vs Exception**: StackOverflowError is an Error (unchecked, unrecoverable) not an Exception
**Typical cause**: Infinite recursion from a recursive method missing a base case
**Stack trace pattern**: Same method repeated hundreds of times in the trace
**Not heap**: Different from OutOfMemoryError; stack is for method calls, heap is for objects
**Fix strategy**: Add a base case to stop recursion, or convert recursive algorithm to iterative

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: StackOverflowError happens when the call stack runs out of space. The call stack is where Java keeps track of method calls — every time you call a method, it pushes a new frame onto the stack, and when the method returns, it pops that frame off. The stack has a fixed size, usually around one megabyte per thread. If you keep calling methods without returning, eventually the stack fills up and you get StackOverflowError. The most common cause is infinite recursion, where a method calls itself over and over without a base case to stop. For example, if you write a factorial function that just returns n times factorial of n minus one, without checking if n is zero or one, it'll recurse forever. The stack trace is super obvious: you'll see the same method name repeated hundreds of times, like calculate at line eight, calculate at line eight, calculate at line eight. That's your clue that recursion is the problem. The fix is to add a base case — a condition that stops the recursion. It's important to know that StackOverflowError is an Error, not an Exception. Errors represent serious problems you shouldn't try to catch. You fix the code instead. Don't confuse it with OutOfMemoryError, which is about the heap running out of space for objects. This is specifically about the call stack.

questions.question: What is a chained exception (exception cause) in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Chained Exceptions in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: A chained exception shows the original cause of an exception when one exception is wrapped inside another, indicated by 'Caused by:' in the stack trace.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to read complex stack traces with multiple exception layers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only reading the first exception and missing the root cause in the 'Caused by:' section
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the root cause is almost always at the bottom of the Caused by chain

sections.title: Exception Cause and Chaining Mechanism
sections.content: A **chained exception** (or exception cause) is Java's mechanism for preserving error context across architectural layers. When low-level code throws an exception (like SQLException from the database), higher layers often catch it and wrap it in a more meaningful business exception (like OrderProcessingException), passing the original exception as the **cause**. This creates a chain: the top exception provides business context ("order 12345 failed"), while the innermost exception reveals the technical root cause ("duplicate key violation"). Java's Throwable class supports this via the **initCause()** method and constructors that accept a cause parameter. The chain appears in stack traces as successive **Caused by:** blocks, each showing a deeper layer of the call. Think of it like nested Russian dolls: you see the outer doll first (high-level business error), but the real problem is the innermost doll (low-level system error). This pattern is ubiquitous in Spring Boot apps where architectural layers (controller, service, repository, JDBC driver) each add context, creating chains four or five exceptions deep. Reading the chain correctly means understanding which layer threw which exception and why.

sections.title: Creating and Reading Chained Exceptions
Key Points
content: **Exception cause**: The original exception that triggered the current exception, creating a parent-child relationship
**Caused by keyword**: Stack trace notation showing the next exception in the chain
**initCause()**: Throwable method that sets the cause after exception construction
**Constructor chaining**: Most exception constructors accept a Throwable cause parameter
**Root cause location**: Always at the bottom of the Caused by chain — the innermost exception
**Layer wrapping**: Each architectural layer catches and rewraps exceptions, adding context
**getCause()**: Method to programmatically retrieve the cause from a Throwable object

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A chained exception is when one exception wraps another, preserving the original error while adding context. This happens constantly in layered applications. Let's say your repository tries to save a record with a duplicate ID. The database driver throws SQLException. Hibernate catches that and wraps it in ConstraintViolationException. Spring Data catches that and wraps it in DataIntegrityViolationException. Your service layer catches that and wraps it in OrderException with a business-friendly message. Each layer adds meaning, but the original technical error is still there. In the stack trace, you see Caused by sections showing each layer. The top exception is your business exception with a message like Failed to create order. Then you see Caused by with Spring's exception. Then another Caused by with Hibernate's exception. Finally, at the very bottom, you see the root cause: the SQLException saying Duplicate entry. That bottom exception is the one you care about for fixing the bug. It tells you exactly what went wrong technically. The top exceptions just add context about where in your code this happened. When reading these, I always scroll to the last Caused by first to see the root technical problem, then work backward to understand how it propagated through my code. The mistake freshers make is stopping at the top exception and missing the real cause at the bottom.

sections.title: Decoding the 'at' Line Format
sections.content: Every line starting with **'at'** in a Java stack trace represents one **stack frame** — a snapshot of a method call at the moment the exception occurred. The format is standardized: **at fully.qualified.ClassName.methodName(SourceFile.java:lineNumber)**. Let's break it down. The **fully qualified class name** shows the package path and class (com.example.order.OrderService). The **method name** is the method that was executing (createOrder). The **source file** (OrderService.java) is the file containing that class. The **line number** (:42) is the exact line in that file where execution was. If the code was compiled without debug symbols, you'll see "Unknown Source" instead of a line number. The 'at' lines form a **reverse chronological call chain**: the top line is where the exception was thrown, the next line is the method that called it, and so on, ending at main() or the framework entry point. Think of it like a crime scene reconstruction: each 'at' line is a step backward in time, showing how execution reached the failure point. For debugging, you scan these lines to find **your code** — the frames containing your package name — because that's where your bug lives.

sections.title: Anatomy of Stack Trace 'at' Lines
Key Points
content: **'at' prefix**: Every stack frame starts with 'at', followed by the method location
**Fully qualified name**: Package path + class name identifies exactly which class (com.example.order.OrderService)
**Line number precision**: The number after the colon (e.g., :42) is the exact line in the source file
**Call chain order**: Top-to-bottom shows newest call (exception throw) to oldest call (main or framework entry)
**Native Method**: Indicates JVM internal code implemented in C/C++, not Java source
**Unknown Source**: Appears when code is compiled without debug info (javac without -g flag)
**IDE integration**: Click any 'at' line in IntelliJ or Eclipse to jump directly to that code

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The at lines in a stack trace are the actual call chain that led to the exception. Each line represents one method call that was active when things went wrong. The format is consistent: at, then the fully qualified class name with package, then the method name, then in parentheses the source file and line number. For example, at com.example.order.OrderService.createOrder means the createOrder method in the OrderService class in the com.example.order package. The part in parentheses, like OrderService.java:42, tells me exactly which file and which line to look at. That colon-42 is where I go in my IDE to see what was happening. The at lines are ordered top-to-bottom by time, with the most recent call at the top. So if the top line is at OrderValidator.validate at line eighteen, that's where the exception was actually thrown. The next line down shows who called validate, and so on. To debug efficiently, I scan down looking for my package name. Framework lines like org.springframework or java.base aren't my code, so I skip them. Once I find my package, I note those line numbers and open those files. That's where my bug is. One tip: if you see Native Method in the parentheses, that's JVM internals you can't debug. And if you see Unknown Source, it means the code was compiled without debug symbols, so you don't get line numbers. But in a normal development environment with your own code, you'll always have the file and line number, making it easy to jump right to the problem.

speakable_v2.hook: Each 'at' line is a breadcrumb — together they trace the exact path your code took before the exception was thrown.

beats.heading: What each line contains
beats.body: The format is: at FullyQualifiedClassName.methodName(FileName.java:lineNumber). The topmost 'at' line is where the exception was actually thrown. Every line below it is the method that called the one above — reading downward shows you how execution got to the throw site.

beats.heading: Practical strategy
items: Read the exception type and message first.
Find the topmost 'at' line that matches your application package.
Open that file at that exact line number.
If unclear, check the next 'at' line in your package — that's the caller.

beats.heading: gotcha
beats.body: If every 'at' line is JDK or framework code with none from your package, the problem is likely a configuration mistake — wrong dependency version, missing bean, or misused API — not a bug in your business logic.

speakable_v2.cap: Top 'at' line in your package is your starting point. IntelliJ makes those lines clickable in the console so you can jump straight to the source.

questions.question: What is a StackOverflowError and what typically causes it?
questions.title: StackOverflowError Causes
questions.direct_answer: StackOverflowError occurs when the call stack exceeds its maximum depth, most commonly caused by infinite or excessively deep recursion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JVM memory and recursion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing StackOverflowError with OutOfMemoryError or not knowing what the call stack is
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what the call stack is and how each method call adds a frame to it

sections.title: Call Stack Overflow and Recursion
sections.content: **StackOverflowError** is thrown when the JVM's **call stack** runs out of space. The call stack is a special memory area where Java tracks active method calls. Each time you invoke a method, Java pushes a **stack frame** onto the stack containing the method's local variables, parameters, and return address. When the method completes, Java pops that frame off. The stack has a fixed maximum size (typically 512 KB to 1 MB per thread, set by the **-Xss JVM flag**). If your code calls methods in a chain that never completes — most often due to **infinite recursion** — the stack keeps growing until it hits the limit, and the JVM throws StackOverflowError. Picture a stack of plates: you keep adding plates (method calls) without removing any (returning from methods). Eventually, the stack topples over. This is fundamentally different from **OutOfMemoryError**, which occurs when the **heap** (where objects live) runs out of space. StackOverflowError is about the depth of your call chain, not the size of your objects. It's an **Error**, not an Exception, signaling a severe problem you typically don't catch — you fix the recursion logic instead.

sections.title: Infinite Recursion Causing StackOverflowError
Key Points
content: **Call stack**: Fixed-size memory region storing method call frames (local variables, return addresses)
**Stack frame**: Data structure pushed onto the stack for each method invocation, popped on return
**Default size**: Usually 512 KB to 1 MB per thread; configurable with -Xss JVM flag (e.g., -Xss2m)
**Infinite recursion**: Most common cause — recursive method lacking a base case to stop
**Stack vs heap**: Stack stores method calls; heap stores objects. StackOverflowError ≠ OutOfMemoryError
**Error classification**: It's an Error (extends Throwable, not Exception), indicating unrecoverable condition
**Stack trace signature**: Same method name repeated hundreds or thousands of times in the trace

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: StackOverflowError happens when the call stack runs out of memory. The call stack is where Java keeps track of which methods are currently executing. Every time you call a method, Java pushes a frame onto the stack with that method's local variables and parameters. When the method returns, Java pops that frame off. The stack has a maximum size, usually around one megabyte per thread, which you can adjust with the -Xss flag when starting the JVM. The most common reason for StackOverflowError is infinite recursion. If you write a recursive method that never hits a base case to stop, it just keeps calling itself, and each call adds another frame to the stack. Eventually, the stack fills up completely and you get the error. For example, if you write a Fibonacci function that calls itself with n minus one and n minus two, but you forget to check if n is zero or one, it'll recurse forever. The stack trace is really obvious: you'll see the same method repeated thousands of times, like calculate at line six, calculate at line six, over and over. That's your signal that recursion is out of control. The fix is to add a base case — a condition that stops the recursion. It's important to know this is different from OutOfMemoryError. OutOfMemoryError is about the heap running out of space for objects. StackOverflowError is specifically about the call stack, which is a separate memory area. And since it's an Error, not an Exception, you don't catch it — you fix your code.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with SLF4J and Logback logging
speakable_v2.hook: StackOverflowError means your code called itself too many times — and the fix is almost always a missing base case.

beats.heading: How the call stack works
beats.body: Every method call pushes a new frame onto the call stack holding local variables and the return address. When the method returns, the frame is popped. The stack has a fixed size — typically a few thousand frames — and infinite recursion fills it completely.

beats.heading: Common causes
items: A recursive method missing a base case — calls itself forever.
Mutual recursion — method A calls B, B calls A, with no termination.
toString or equals calling itself indirectly through object relationships.

beats.heading: sharp edge
beats.body: StackOverflowError is in the java.lang.Error hierarchy, not Exception. Catching it with a catch block is technically possible but almost always wrong — it signals a broken algorithm that needs to be fixed, not swallowed.

speakable_v2.cap: Look for the repeating method name in the trace, find the missing or broken base case, and fix the recursion. For very deep legitimate trees, convert to iterative with an explicit stack.
